confidence_interval.rationale: I am reasonably confident (moderate-to-high) in the descriptive and critical assessment based on the manuscript and shared analysis; uncertainty remains due to limited scale of live experiments, missing operational details (cost/latency), and lack of robustness ablations under noisy feedback and entity-matching failures.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes an end-to-end, low-engineering pipeline to learn NL->SQL semantic parsers: (1) a standard attention-based seq2seq model decodes anonymized utterances directly to full SQL; (2) schema-agnostic SQL templates plus PPDB-based paraphrasing bootstrap initial training data; (3) TF-IDF entity span matching anonymizes/fills entities; (4) an online train-deploy-feedback loop collects coarse user feedback and routes incorrect cases to crowd workers for full SQL annotation. Empirical evidence spans denotational benchmark experiments (GEO880, ATIS), simulated interactive learning (perfect feedback), and a small live three-stage deployment on an academic DB producing the SCHOLAR dataset (816 SQL-labeled utterances). The manuscript's chain of reasoning is that seq2seq models are expressive enough for SQL, that schema-agnostic augmentation yields useful seeds to motivate early user interactions, and that cheap user feedback + selective crowd annotation yields rapid bootstrapping and continued improvement with reduced annotation effort. Evidence in the paper supports component-level effectiveness (notably paraphrasing helps, templates help certain domains, TF-IDF enables flexible matching) and demonstrates feasibility in a small live setting, but several claims of generality and operational efficiency rest on limited-scale experiments, optimistic simulations (perfect feedback), and qualitative/partial quantification (crowd cost/latency, sensitivity to entity-matching noise). I flag uncertainties, provide alternative interpretations, and give specific suggestions and tests to strengthen the causal claims.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Standard seq2seq + attention can produce SQL tokens from anonymized NL (Section 4.1).
A2: Schema-agnostic templates can instantiate executable SQL and paired utterances (Section 4.3).
A3: Paraphrase augmentation expands surface variability and improves generalization (Section 4.3, 5.3).
A4: TF-IDF entity span retrieval enables anonymization at test time and post-hoc filling (Section 4.2).

A5: Deploy early model to collect user feedback (Correct/Incomplete vs Incorrect); accepted predictions added directly to training; incorrect predictions sent to crowd for full SQL (Algorithm 1, Section 3).
A6: Iterative retraining with added (n,q) and crowd-labeled (n,q̂) reduces annotation effort and improves denotation accuracy over stages (Section 6.2, 6.4).
A7: Benchmarks show near-state-of-the-art denotation accuracy without schema-specific features (Section 5.3).
A8: Small live deployment (3 stages, 30 users) raised correct/incomplete fraction from ~25% to ~63.5% and produced SCHOLAR (Section 6.2, 6.3).
Conclusion: The integrated pipeline is a practical, low-engineering approach to bootstrap NLIDBs via user feedback + selective crowdsourcing.

identified_claims.claim_text: A sequence-to-sequence neural model with attention can directly generate full SQL queries from natural language and achieve accuracy comparable to prior semantic parsers on GEO880 and ATIS without database-specific feature engineering.
evidence: Section 5.3: Tables 2 and 3 report denotation accuracies (e.g., 82.5% on GEO880) and comparison with prior work.
Model description (Section 4.1): encoder-decoder with global attention, pretrained word2vec, beam search.
uncertainty_flags: Comparisons are qualitative in parts; best-performing non-SQL systems (e.g., Jia & Liang) still show higher accuracies — the claim of 'comparable' depends on which baselines are considered.
Preprocessing choices (e.g., converting IN to JOIN) and small percentages of empty-result gold queries may affect direct comparability.

identified_claims.claim_text: An interactive feedback loop that deploys a preliminary model, collects binary user feedback on query results, and selectively sends incorrect cases for crowd annotation enables rapid bootstrapping and continued improvement of a semantic parser in a new domain with minimal intervention.
evidence: Algorithm 1 explicitly describes adding user-validated (n,q) to training and sending incorrect ones to crowd for q̂.
Three-stage live experiment (Section 6.2) reports improvement from 25% to 63.51% correct/incomplete.
uncertainty_flags: Live experiment is small (30 users total, 3 stages), limiting external validity for 'rapid' bootstrapping claims across diverse domains.
Operational metrics (annotation latency, monetary cost, crowd inter-annotator agreement) are not provided, so 'minimal intervention' is not fully quantified.
Simulated experiments assume perfect feedback and are optimistic relative to noisy user feedback observed (~6% miscues).

identified_claims.claim_text: Schema-agnostic template-based synthetic data plus paraphrase-based augmentation provide viable initial training data that enable useful early-stage performance and reduce annotation effort.
evidence: 22 templates instantiated via schema graphs to produce executable SQL and anonymized utterances (Section 4.3).
Live stage 1 (templates+paraphrases only) achieved 25% correct (Section 6.2).
Simulated experiments show templates help GEO880 early stages; paraphrasing consistently helps (Section 6.4).
uncertainty_flags: Templates did not help ATIS (Section 6.4), indicating domain-dependence of this claim.
Paraphrasing method (random single-word replacement using PPDB) may introduce semantic drift; quality control is not deeply analyzed.

identified_claims.claim_text: Entity anonymization via TF-IDF lookup combined with post-hoc filling of generated SQL supports flexible entity handling across domains.
evidence: Method describes span-wise TF-IDF retrieval over DB entity names and replacement with typed placeholders; mappings stored to fill SQL.
Qualitative example handling 'Donald Knuth' vs 'Donald E. Knuth'.
uncertainty_flags: Empirical impact on end-to-end denotation accuracy and failure modes (ambiguous spans, misspellings, rare entities) is not quantitatively isolated.
Feedback category 'Wrong Types' is reported but not tied to precise TF-IDF failure rates.

identified_claims.claim_text: User-provided binary/multi-option feedback has low enough error rates (e.g., ~6% false negatives/positives) to permit effective learning from interaction.
evidence: Table 6: Final-stage measured feedback error rates: 6.1% of correct SQL marked wrong and 6.3% of incorrect SQL marked correct.
Section 6.2: authors state this feedback quality suffices for improvement.
uncertainty_flags: Error rates measured only in final stage; may vary across stages and user populations.
Effect of these errors on long-run model drift or biased errors is not experimentally quantified.

identified_claims.claim_text: A small live deployment for an academic papers database demonstrates practical feasibility: after three train-deploy cycles the system's proportion of correct/incomplete answers increased substantially (to ~63.5%), and a new SCHOLAR dataset (816 utterances with SQL) is produced and released.
evidence: Section 6.2: reported stage-wise correctness numbers culminating in 63.51%.
Section 6.3: SCHOLAR dataset described (816 utterances, 600/216 split) and parser achieves 67% supervised accuracy.
uncertainty_flags: Live deployment involved only 30 users and additional crowd-labeled utterances not from the live run were included in the released dataset—this complicates claims about dataset provenance and 'learning from live usage alone.'
Generalizability and longer-term stability beyond three days/stages is unexplored.

identified_claims.claim_text: Paraphrasing using PPDB consistently improves model performance (both in batch and interactive settings).
evidence: Ablations and experiments (Section 5.3, Section 6.4) report consistent gains when PPDB paraphrasing is applied to training data.
Paraphrase procedure applied to both seed and newly labeled examples.
uncertainty_flags: Magnitude of improvement and statistical significance are not fully enumerated in text; paraphrase quality via single-word substitution may introduce noisy examples.
Improvement appears robust in presented experiments but may depend on domain lexical distributions.

strengths.title: End-to-end, deployable pipeline
strengths.description: Presents a practical, modular pipeline (seq2seq SQL model, anonymization, template seeding, paraphrasing, feedback loop, crowd annotation) that can be implemented with modest engineering effort.
evidence: Algorithm 1 formalizes the loop; Sections 4 and 6 detail components and a working web UI was used for live tests.

strengths.title: Empirical validation at multiple levels
strengths.description: Evaluation covers batch benchmarks (GEO880, ATIS), simulated interactive experiments, and a small live deployment, supporting feasibility claims across controlled and real settings.
evidence: Section 5: benchmark results; Section 6.4: simulated batch dynamics; Section 6.2: three-stage live experiment.

strengths.title: Low-engineering schema-agnostic seeding
strengths.description: Schema templates instantiated via schema graph shortest paths produce executable SQL seeds that are portable across schemas without hand-crafting domain rules.
evidence: Section 4.3: 22 templates, shortest-path join generation example (Figure 2).
Stage-1 live performance (25% correct) indicates usefulness of seeds in practice.

strengths.title: Practical entity handling strategy
strengths.description: A simple TF-IDF based entity span retrieval plus anonymization and post-hoc filling trades complex NER engineering for a lightweight, schema-driven approach.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes progressive span TF-IDF matching and placeholder replacement; explicit discussion of mapping stored for SQL filling.

strengths.title: Dataset and artifacts released
strengths.description: Provides the SCHOLAR dataset and processed benchmark versions, enabling reproducibility and follow-up work.
evidence: Section 5.1: processed GEO/ATIS will be released; Section 6.3: SCHOLAR dataset description (816 utterances).

concerns.title: Limited scale and external validity of live deployment
concerns.description: The three-stage live experiment involved only 30 users (10 per stage) and a short timespan; this small scale weakens claims that the approach 'rapidly' bootstraps or generalizes to diverse real-world deployments.
evidence: Section 6.2: experiment recruited 10 new users per stage for 3 stages; total 30 users.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers note small-scale nature and limited diversity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either (a) report per-user demographics and per-utterance length/type distributions to contextualize the sample, or (b) run an extended deployment with more users and longer duration (or report retrospective logs showing stability across time).

concerns.title: Simulations assume perfect feedback, optimistic dynamics
concerns.description: Simulated interactive experiments provide perfect feedback by comparing predicted results to gold queries; this likely overestimates real-world gains since real user feedback is noisy and contains distinct error modes.
evidence: Section 6.4: simulated experiments use gold-query denotation comparison for correctness.
Section 6.2: measured user feedback error rates (~6%) indicate real feedback is imperfect.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run simulations that inject measured noise rates and patterns from the live experiment (e.g., 6% false positives, 6% false negatives, and specific Wrong Types/Incompletes) to quantify performance degradation and robustness.

concerns.title: Insufficient quantification of crowd annotation process and cost
concerns.description: The pipeline relies on sending incorrect cases to crowd workers for SQL annotation, but the paper lacks quantitative details on annotation latency, per-example monetary cost, annotator expertise required, and inter-annotator agreement — all critical to operational feasibility.
evidence: Section 3 and 6.2 describe using crowd workers but do not provide cost/latency/agreement metrics.
Shared analysis and prior-stage reviewers note missing operational quantification.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide statistics from the crowdsourcing runs: time-to-first-annotation, average time per SQL, pay rates, quality checks (e.g., agreement, verification steps), and examples of ambiguous cases requiring adjudication.

concerns.title: Entity-matching robustness not isolated
concerns.description: TF-IDF entity retrieval is presented as effective, but there is limited quantitative analysis of failure modes (ambiguous spans, low-frequency entities, typos) and their downstream impact on denotation accuracy and annotation load.
evidence: Section 4.2 describes the TF-IDF scheme; Section 6.2 reports Wrong Types feedback but no ablation tying it to TF-IDF.
Shared analysis recommends conditioning accuracy on entity-matching quality.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report an ablation where entity anonymization is disabled or replaced with oracle matching on a subset, measure denotation accuracy conditioned on matching confidence, and describe fallback heuristics used in ambiguous cases.

concerns.title: Paraphrase augmentation quality control
concerns.description: Paraphrasing is done by single random non-stopword replacement with PPDB paraphrases — this can produce semantic drift or ungrammatical examples; paper lacks analyses on paraphrase-induced noise or gating mechanisms.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes random single-word replacement using PPDB large set; claimed benefit in Section 5.3 and 6.4.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers note possible semantic corruption risk.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report the proportion of paraphrases that change denotation (manual sample), include confidence filtering (PPDB score threshold), or use paraphrase templates preserving entity types; provide ablations with varying paraphrase quality settings.

concerns.title: Benchmark comparison and preprocessing clarity
concerns.description: Some preprocessing choices (e.g., converting IN to JOIN) and handling of gold queries with empty results are noted but not fully enumerated numerically; this can affect fairness of comparisons to prior work.
evidence: Section 5.1: mentions IN->JOIN conversion and that 2.8% GEO880 and 5% ATIS gold queries produce empty results.
Section 5.3 contrasts to prior work but detailed numeric baselines and statistical tests are limited.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide full tables of numeric comparisons with explicit notes on preprocessing for each baseline, and include statistical significance testing or confidence intervals where possible.

concerns.title: Training label quality risk from erroneous 'accepted' feedback
concerns.description: Users sometimes mark incorrect SQL as correct (~6.3%); these false acceptances will be added directly to training as (n,q) and could bias or degrade model performance over time — the paper does not analyze long-run effects.
evidence: Table 6: 6.3% of incorrect SQL were erroneously labeled correct by users.
Algorithm 1: accepted (n,q) are added to training without further verification.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Propose and evaluate safeguards: e.g., detect high-loss or low-confidence accepted examples and route them for verification, maintain a validation hold-out, or weight user-accepted examples differently during optimization; simulate/deploy such strategies and report effects.

comparable_works.relevance: High; neural seq2seq/data-recombination advances on semantic parsing used as a comparison point for accuracy improvements and augmentation compatibility.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar neural approach but targeted at logical forms with data recombination; reported higher accuracies on benchmarks using recombination which could be applied to this model.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 5.3 references Jia and Liang (2016) as providing data recombination that could boost performance.

comparable_works.relevance: High; neural sequence-to-sequence for logical forms provides context for model expressivity and baseline performance.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar seq2seq mapping but to simpler meaning representations rather than full SQL; the present paper extends to SQL generation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 5.3 cites Dong and Lapata as relevant neural sequence-based approaches.

comparable_works.citation_label: Popescu et al. (2003); Giordani & Moschitti (2012); Poon (2013)
comparable_works.relevance: Medium; prior systems that directly produce SQL but constrained by engineered rules or limited SQL subsets.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Differ in level of engineering: prior systems often rely on strong lexical matches/rules; current paper emphasizes minimal schema-specific engineering and neural generation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Related work discussion (Section 2) and Section 5.3 comparisons.

comparable_works.relevance: High; used directly for paraphrase augmentation in this work.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: PPDB is an external resource; paper adopts a simple sampling strategy rather than more structured paraphrase generation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 4.3 describes using PPDB for paraphrasing.

uncertainty_flags: Small scale of live deployment (30 users) limits external validity for claims of rapid bootstrapping across domains.
Simulations assume perfect user feedback and may overestimate gains compared to noisy real users.
Crowd annotation cost/latency/quality metrics are missing, leaving operational feasibility uncertain.
TF-IDF entity matching failure modes and their quantitative impact are undercharacterized.
Paraphrase augmentation may introduce semantic noise; quality control measures are limited.
alternative_interpretations: The observed improvements across interactive stages could be driven primarily by a small fraction of high-impact crowd-labeled examples rather than the general self-training of accepted predictions; ablations that exclude user-accepted (n,q) vs crowd (n,q̂) would clarify contributions.
Stage-wise improvement may partly reflect overfitting to a narrow user population or the particular academic schema; larger, more diverse user sets might yield slower gains.

Template seeds may mainly contribute to early user engagement (interface perception) rather than model representational readiness; the 25% stage-1 performance could equally reflect templated utterances being common among early users.
transparency_notes: The paper provides architecture and algorithmic detail (model equations, Algorithm 1, template instantiation) but omits quantitative operational metrics for crowd annotation (cost/latency/quality) and limited statistical testing on benchmark comparisons.

SCHOLAR dataset provenance mixes live-collected utterances and additional crowd-labeled utterances; the paper notes that added crowd examples were not used in the live run but are included in the released set—clarify which subsets originate from live interaction.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While the overall integration (seq2seq-to-SQL + schema-agnostic templates + TF-IDF anonymization + live user feedback + crowd annotation) appears relatively novel as a combined pipeline, novelty alone doesn't guarantee robustness; operational scalability and robustness to noisy feedback remain empirical questions.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If crowd annotations are high-quality, low-latency, and inexpensive, the loop will scale and bootstrapping gains observed will generalize.
If entity TF-IDF matching maintains high precision on common user spans (e.g., representative user expressions), anonymization will minimize entity-induced errors and training noise.
If paraphrase augmentation is filtered by confidence (PPDB scores) or semantic validation, it will consistently improve generalization without adding harmful noise.

If user populations provide feedback with error rates comparable to measured (~6%), the system can tolerate noise; but if feedback error rates are much higher, model degradation may occur unless safeguards are implemented.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Components (seq2seq models, paraphrase augmentation, simple entity anonymization, interactive feedback) are individually known; their tight integration into a lightweight, schema-agnostic NLIDB bootstrapping loop and demonstration on a live system is the novel engineering contribution.
evidence: Paper ties together these components and demonstrates a working live loop (Algorithm 1, Section 6.2).
uncertainty_flags: Integration novelty depends on prior art degree (some prior systems generated SQL; some used feedback); absence of direct prior integrated systems in literature increases novelty but exact novelty margin is qualitative.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Seq2seq-to-program generation and data augmentation via paraphrases have precedents; TF-IDF anonymization is a pragmatic heuristic rather than a new algorithmic method.
evidence: Related work cites neural program generation and paraphrasing literature; Sections 2 and 4 build on these methods.
uncertainty_flags: Combining these known methods into a production-oriented loop with crowd-in-the-loop may nonetheless be valuable in practice.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper frames a low-engineering pathway to fielding NLIDBs that could lower barriers to building domain-specific natural language interfaces, which is a useful and potentially disruptive practical shift.
evidence: Live deployment and SCHOLAR dataset release demonstrate applied viability; emphasis on minimal schema-specific engineering makes solution attractive to practitioners.
uncertainty_flags: Whether this approach disrupts current NLIDB practices depends on scalability (crowd costs, entity matching robustness) which remain empirically underexplored.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects epistemic uncertainty: high confidence in paper's reported internal results (benchmarks, live small-scale trial, and described methods) but lower confidence in generalization claims due to limited live sample size, optimistic simulations, and missing operational quantification (crowd cost/latency, entity-match failure rates). The interval encodes moderate-to-high belief that core feasibility claims hold in similar constrained settings but uncertainty about broader scalability and robustness.

consensus_findings: A standard attention-based sequence-to-sequence model can be trained to generate executable SQL from natural language and attains competitive denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS in the authors' experimental setup.

An end-to-end pipeline integrating schema-agnostic templates, PPDB-based paraphrase augmentation, TF-IDF entity anonymization, user feedback, and selective crowd annotation is feasible to implement and was demonstrated in a small live deployment that produced the SCHOLAR dataset.
Paraphrase-based data augmentation consistently yields empirical gains across settings reported by the authors.

Schema-agnostic templates can provide useful early-stage seed data in some domains (e.g., the academic SCHOLAR setting and GEO880) but their effectiveness is domain-dependent (not helpful for ATIS in the reported simulations).

User-provided feedback is informative and can be used to add training pairs; measured user-feedback error rates in the live trial (~6% false positives and ~6% false negatives in the final stage) are non-negligible but were judged by authors to be tolerable for improvement in the reported setting.

TF-IDF based entity anonymization is a pragmatic, lightweight approach that enables schema-agnostic anonymization/filling in the pipeline, and it worked sufficiently in the authors' live demo, but its robustness to varied failure modes is not deeply quantified.
disagreements: Scale and generality of the interactive bootstrapping claim: reviewers agree the small live deployment shows feasibility, but disagree on whether the evidence suffices to support claims about rapid bootstrapping 'in new domains' broadly. Some characterize this as an existence proof (novel, applied); others view broader claims as premature without larger-scale trials.

Degree to which template seeding is a broadly effective strategy: reviewers concur templates helped some domains but disagree on presenting them as generally reliable; ATIS negative result prompted caution that template utility is domain-dependent.

Interpretation of simulated interactive experiments: reviewers accept simulations as informative for controlled exploration but disagree about their external validity because simulations assume perfect feedback and hence likely overestimate real-world gains.

Operational feasibility of crowd annotation: reviewers agree crowd annotation is plausible, but disagree on whether the provided qualitative description suffices to claim 'minimal intervention' at scale—some request quantitative cost/latency/QA metrics to support operational claims.
uncertainty_hotspots: External validity of live deployment: small sample (30 users across 3 stages) — uncertainty about performance trajectory, user heterogeneity effects, and long-term model behavior in larger or different deployments.

Impact of noisy user feedback on long-term model quality: measured ~6% erroneous accept/decline rates; uncertainty about cumulative effects of incorrectly accepted SQL added to training and potential model drift.

Entity-matching robustness: TF-IDF retrieval behavior under ambiguous mentions, misspellings, low-frequency entities, and multi-token referents is under-characterized; downstream effect on Wrong Types errors and denotation accuracy is uncertain.

Paraphrase quality and semantic drift: single-word PPDB substitutions may introduce meaning shifts; uncertainty about fraction of paraphrases that preserve denotation and their net effect across domains.
Annotation economics and latency: lack of reported per-example time, monetary cost, inter-annotator agreement, and stage-to-stage latency creates operational uncertainty for practical deployment.

Benchmark comparability details: preprocessing choices (e.g., IN->JOIN conversion), excluded/empty-result gold queries, and limited reporting of statistical variance raise uncertainty about head-to-head comparability to the strongest prior systems.
model_diversity_effects: Different reviewers emphasize different aspects (logical-coherence, reproducibility, incremental novelty, disruptive framing), which affects emphasis on weaknesses vs. novelty: methodology-focused reviewers highlight missing reproducibility/operational metrics (cost, latency, ablations), while novelty/engineering-focused reviewers treat the integrated pipeline and live demo as the core contribution despite those gaps.

This diversity reveals role-specific sensitivity: structure/logic reviewers flag causal attribution risks when multiple components interact (templates + anonymization + crowd-in-the-loop), methodology auditors prioritize ablations and variance reporting, and novelty assessors weigh integration novelty more heavily than algorithmic novelty.

Taken together, the reviewer ensemble suggests the work's strength is applied integration; the ensemble variance indicates the manuscript would benefit from additional targeted analyses to satisfy distinct concerns (robustness, reproducibility, operational economics).
meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat the manuscript as an applied, integrative empirical contribution that demonstrates a promising pipeline and a small live proof-of-concept. The central decision-maker (editor) should request revisions focused on clarifying and quantifying operational and robustness aspects rather than asking for fundamentally new modeling work. Specifically, ask authors to (1) provide quantitative annotation metrics (per-example crowd cost, median latency, number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, qualification/filtering procedures); (2) run and report ablations that isolate entity-matching (disable/replace TF-IDF) and measure how entity-matching errors affect denotation accuracy and Wrong Types feedback rates; (3) include simulations that inject realistic feedback noise (reflecting measured ~6% error rates) and analyze sensitivity of learning curves to feedback error; (4) expand reporting of benchmark comparisons with exact preprocessing steps, full numeric tables, variance estimates (e.g., multiple seeds or bootstrap CIs) and per-query failure examples; and (5) provide paraphrase-quality diagnostics (sample error analysis, PPDB score thresholds or conservative paraphrase variants) and, if possible, an expanded live or replay-based experiment to assess generalization or variability across user cohorts. Keep reviewers' controlled disagreements visible in the decision record: the evidence shows feasibility but not yet general scalability.
meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewers' concerns and strengthen claims, please provide the following additions or clarifications: (1) Operational annotation statistics: per-utterance annotation time, monetary cost, number of annotators per example, inter-annotator agreement/QA process, and wall-clock latency between stages in the live run. (2) Robustness ablations: an experiment (or held-out analysis) that measures end-to-end denotation accuracy conditioned on TF-IDF entity-matching success, and an ablation where anonymization is disabled or replaced with oracle matching to quantify its contribution. (3) Feedback-noise sensitivity: simulated retraining curves with injected realistic feedback noise matching observed error profiles (false-positive/negative rates and 'Wrong Types' patterns); evaluate mitigations such as confidence thresholds or sampled verification. (4) Paraphrase diagnostics: manual or automatic evaluation of paraphrase fidelity on a sample (fraction that preserves denotation), and ablations with more conservative paraphrase selection (e.g., PPDB score cutoffs). (5) Benchmark transparency: publish all SQL preprocessing scripts, exact dataset splits, full numeric result tables (per-dataset, per-condition), and variance measures (repeats or bootstrap CIs). (6) Dataset provenance: clearly state which SCHOLAR utterances were collected from live users vs. added via crowd annotation, and provide an appendix with annotation instructions and examples. Where practical, supplement the paper with either a larger-scale or replay-based interactive experiment to demonstrate robustness across user variability.
transparency_report: Provided: model architecture details (encoder-decoder with global attention), training hyperparameters, high-level descriptions of template generation and paraphrasing procedure, and promise to release processed GEO/ATIS and SCHOLAR artifacts — these materially support reproducibility.

Missing or under-specified: template instantiation scripts and coverage statistics, TF-IDF index construction parameters and retrieval thresholds, paraphrase sampling random seeds and PPDB subset/score thresholds, crowd annotation protocol (instructions, qualification criteria, pay, per-item latency), and full numeric ablation tables with variance estimates.

Simulation assumptions: simulated interactive experiments assume perfect oracle feedback; this assumption and its implications are described but its optimism relative to measured user noise should be explicitly signposted and alternative noisy simulations provided.

Dataset provenance: the SCHOLAR release mixes live-collected and crowd-annotated examples; the exact composition and which examples were used in live retraining should be explicitly documented in released metadata.
epistemic_limits: The evidence supports that the integrated pipeline can work in constrained settings and that seq2seq models can generate executable SQL with competitive denotation accuracy under the authors' preprocessing and training regime. However, the study's small live sample size, optimistic simulation assumptions, and missing operational metrics limit confidence in claims of rapid, low-cost bootstrapping across arbitrary new domains. Causal attribution among interacting components (templates vs. paraphrasing vs. entity anonymization vs. crowd annotation) is only partially resolved by the presented ablations and requires targeted isolation experiments. Additionally, denotation-based evaluation may hide semantic mismatches that happen to produce the correct result on the current database snapshot. These epistemic limits mean that positive results should be interpreted as a promising proof-of-concept and engineering recipe rather than definitive evidence of scalable, general-purpose NLIDB bootstrapping without further robustness and operational validation.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: This manuscript presents an end-to-end engineering pipeline for mapping natural language to executable SQL using a standard attention-based sequence-to-sequence model, schema-agnostic SQL templates plus PPDB paraphrase augmentation to seed training, TF-IDF entity anonymization/filling, and an online train-deploy-feedback loop where user feedback is used to accept model outputs and incorrect cases are routed to crowd workers for SQL annotation. Evidence includes denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS (reported as comparable to prior parsers under the authors' preprocessing), simulated interactive experiments (oracle feedback), and a small live three-stage deployment on an academic database that produced the SCHOLAR dataset and increased the correct/incomplete response fraction from ~25% to ~63.5%. Reviewers agree the paper is a coherent, practical systems contribution demonstrating feasibility, but identify important limitations in scale, robustness analyses, and operational quantification.
strengths: Demonstrates a complete, implementable NL->SQL pipeline integrating modeling, anonymization, seeding, paraphrasing, feedback collection, and selective crowdsourced annotation, and releases artifacts (processed benchmarks and SCHOLAR).
Shows that a generic attention-based seq2seq decoder can produce full SQL with competitive denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS under the reported setup (no DB-specific feature engineering).

Presents pragmatic augmentation strategies (schema-agnostic templates instantiated via schema graph shortest paths and PPDB-based paraphrasing) that empirically improve early-stage performance in some domains, and provides UI/feedback taxonomy design and measured user feedback error rates from a live trial.
limitations: Live deployment scale and external validity: the online experiment comprised only three stages with 10 new users per stage (≈30 users total). Claims about rapid, low-intervention bootstrapping across new domains rest on this small sample and are not yet demonstrated at larger scales or varied user populations.

Optimistic simulation assumptions and incomplete robustness checks: interactive simulations assume perfect oracle feedback; real user feedback is noisy (~6% false positives/negatives measured) and the paper lacks sensitivity analyses showing how feedback noise affects learning curves and potential model drift.

Entity-matching and anonymization not fully ablated: TF-IDF span retrieval is central to portability claims but the manuscript lacks quantitative ablations showing how entity-matching errors propagate to denotation accuracy, Wrong Types feedback rates, and annotation workload.

Operational annotation economics and latency under-specified: key operational claims ("minimal intervention") depend on crowd annotation cost, per-item latency, annotator qualifications and inter-annotator agreement, none of which are reported quantitatively.
open_questions: Please provide per-example crowd-annotation metrics from the live run: median annotation latency, monetary cost per SQL, number of annotators per example, inter-annotator agreement or QA checks, and wall-clock time between stages.

Provide robustness simulations where realistic user-feedback noise (e.g., the measured ~6% false accept/reject rates and observed 'Wrong Types' patterns) is injected: how do learning curves, annotation fraction, and long-run model quality change?

Include an ablation that isolates entity-anonymization: disable TF-IDF anonymization or replace it with oracle matching on a held-out subset to quantify its contribution and report TF-IDF precision/recall on mention-to-entity mapping (including edge cases: abbreviations, typos, partial mentions).

Give concrete paraphrase-quality diagnostics: what fraction of sampled PPDB single-word substitutions preserve the intended denotation (manual spot-check), and do more conservative paraphrase-selection thresholds or filtering change results materially?
consensus_snapshot: Seq2seq with attention can be trained to output full SQL and attains competitive denotation accuracy on GEO880 and ATIS in the authors' experimental setup.

The integrated pipeline (templates + paraphrasing + TF-IDF anonymization + feedback + selective crowdsourcing) is a practical and novel engineering contribution; the live three-stage demo provides an existence proof.
Paraphrase augmentation (PPDB-based) yields consistent empirical gains in the experiments reported; templates help early-stage bootstrapping in some domains but effects are domain-dependent.
disagreement_snapshot: Whether the small live deployment suffices to support claims of rapid bootstrapping across arbitrary new domains: some reviewers treat the demo as a meaningful proof-of-concept, others consider broader claims premature without larger-scale evidence.

How strongly to present template seeding as a general strategy: reviewers agree templates help in some settings (SCHOLAR, GEO880) but disagree about presenting them as broadly reliable—ATIS results show templates can be ineffective.

Degree to which simulated interactive experiments inform real-world deployment: reviewers differ on the weight given to oracle-feedback simulations versus the noisy live-feedback measurements; some see simulations as exploratory, others find their optimism problematic without noisy variants.
uncertainty_snapshot: Operational scalability: uncertainty about crowd annotation cost, latency, quality-control and how these scale with load.
Long-term effect of noisy accepted labels: measured ~6% of incorrect SQL were accepted by users; uncertainty about cumulative model drift when such errors are added into training across many cycles.
Entity anonymization robustness: TF-IDF matching's behavior on ambiguous, partial, or misspelled mentions and its end-to-end impact are insufficiently quantified.
Benchmark comparability: preprocessing choices (e.g., IN->JOIN conversion) and omitted statistical-variance reporting leave head-to-head comparisons with strongest prior systems somewhat uncertain.
source_trace: Dong, L. & Lapata, M. (2016) — neural seq2seq semantic parsing; used as baseline comparison for encoder-decoder approaches cited in paper (Section 5.3).
Jia, R. & Liang, P. (2016) — data recombination for neural semantic parsing and strong benchmark results; discussed as augmentation alternative (Section 5.3).
Ganitkevitch, J., Van Durme, B., & Callison-Burch, C. (2013) — PPDB paraphrase resource used by authors for single-word paraphrase augmentation (Section 4.3).

Paper's Algorithm 1 and Sections 3, 4.1-4.3, 5, 6 — describe the feedback loop, model, anonymization, templates/paraphrasing, benchmarks and live experiment; reviewers repeatedly reference these sections when requesting ablations or operational details.

Reviewer-requested robustness checks and best-practice guidelines: simulate feedback noise (measured ~6% user error rates, Table 6) and report ablations that isolate TF-IDF impact and paraphrase fidelity (as recommended across specialist reviews).
transparency_notes: Provided materials: model architecture, core hyperparameters, high-level descriptions of template generation and paraphrasing procedure, and promises to release processed GEO/ATIS and the SCHOLAR dataset and DB. Missing or under-specified items that impede exact reproduction of the interactive results: template instantiation scripts and coverage statistics; TF-IDF index construction parameters, tokenization and span-preprocessing rules; PPDB subset/score thresholds, random seeds and paraphrase sampling rates; crowd-annotation instructions, qualification criteria, pay, per-item latency and inter-annotator agreement; full numeric ablation tables with variance estimates and per-query failure examples; and exact SQL preprocessing scripts (IN->JOIN conversions).
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Treat this work as a substantive, applied systems contribution that provides a practical recipe for bootstrapping NL->SQL interfaces and a small live proof-of-concept. Revisions should focus on strengthening operational and robustness evidence rather than new modeling work. Specifically request the authors to: (1) report detailed crowdsourcing metrics (per-item time, cost, annotator agreement/QA procedures, stage-to-stage wall-clock latency); (2) add robustness ablations isolating TF-IDF entity-matching contribution and report retrieval precision/recall on mentions including edge cases; (3) run interactive simulations with injected realistic feedback noise matching measured user error profiles and analyze mitigation strategies (confidence thresholds, sampled verification); (4) provide paraphrase-fidelity diagnostics and, if helpful, a conservative paraphrasing ablation; and (5) publish full numeric benchmark tables, preprocessing scripts, and variance estimates. Maintain visibility of reviewer disagreements: the paper is a convincing proof-of-concept but not yet evidence of general, low-cost scalability without the requested operational analyses.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewer concerns and strengthen causal/generalization claims, please (a) provide per-annotation crowd metrics from your live run: median and distribution of annotation latency, monetary cost per annotated SQL, number of annotators per item, and inter-annotator agreement/quality-control procedure; (b) release scripts for SQL preprocessing (IN->JOIN), template instantiation code, TF-IDF index construction and retrieval thresholds, and paraphrase sampling code with seeds and PPDB subset/score choices; (c) run ablations that (i) disable/replace TF-IDF anonymization (oracle vs none) to quantify its contribution to denotation accuracy and 'Wrong Types' feedback rates, and (ii) compare with/without paraphrase filtering or conservative paraphrase subsets; (d) run simulated interactive experiments with injected realistic feedback noise matching your measured error rates (and explore mitigations such as confidence-based filtering or periodic verification), and report how learning curves and annotation fractions degrade; (e) clearly document which SCHOLAR examples origin from live users versus crowd-added utterances and include annotation instructions and examples in an appendix; and (f) include full numeric result tables, per-condition sample sizes and variance estimates (multiple seeds or bootstrap CIs) and representative failure-case analyses illustrating common error modes.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: This paper presents a practical end-to-end pipeline for NL->SQL that combines an attention-based seq2seq SQL decoder, TF-IDF entity anonymization/filling, schema-agnostic SQL templates plus PPDB-based paraphrasing to seed training, and an online loop where user feedback accepts model outputs and incorrect cases are routed to crowd workers for SQL annotation. Evidence includes denotation benchmark results (GEO880, ATIS), oracle-feedback simulations, and a small live three-stage deployment producing the SCHOLAR dataset and raising correct/incomplete answers from ~25% to ~63.5%.

Strengths: (1) Coherent, implementable integration of modeling, anonymization, seeding, augmentation and human-in-the-loop procedures with artifacts released; (2) Demonstrates that a generic seq2seq model can output full SQL with competitive denotation accuracy under the authors' preprocessing; (3) Practical augmentation (templates + PPDB paraphrasing) and UI/feedback taxonomy design supported by measured live feedback error rates.

Limitations: (1) Live deployment is small-scale (≈30 users across 3 stages), limiting external validity for broad claims about rapid bootstrapping across arbitrary domains; (2) Simulations assume perfect feedback and do not quantify sensitivity to realistic noisy user feedback (measured ~6% errors), leaving uncertainty about long-run model drift when erroneous accepted labels are added; (3) TF-IDF entity anonymization is central but lacks quantitative ablation tying entity matching success/failure to denotation accuracy and annotation load; (4) Crowd annotation economics and latency (cost per SQL, annotation time, agreement) are not reported, so operational feasibility claims are under-supported.

Open Questions: (1) What were the per-example crowd annotation latency, monetary cost, number of annotators per example, and inter-annotator agreement in the live run? (2) How do interactive learning curves and annotation fractions change when realistic feedback noise (the measured ~6% false accepts/rejects and Wrong Types patterns) is injected into simulations? (3) What is the TF-IDF mention-to-entity precision/recall on a held-out mention set (including typos, partial names, ambiguous mentions), and how does disabling TF-IDF anonymization change end-to-end denotation accuracy? (4) What fraction of PPDB single-word substitutions preserve the gold denotation (manual spot-check), and do more conservative paraphrase-selection thresholds materially change results?

Transparency: The manuscript supplies model architecture, hyperparameters, and high-level descriptions of templates/paraphrasing, and announces release of processed benchmarks and SCHOLAR. Missing items that reviewers requested for reproducibility and operational assessment include template instantiation code and coverage stats, TF-IDF index parameters and span-preprocessing rules, PPDB subset/score thresholds and random seeds, crowd annotation instructions/qualification, per-item cost/latency/quality metrics, full numeric ablation tables with variance estimates, and exact SQL preprocessing scripts. Clarifying these will materially strengthen reproducibility and the operational claims.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately to fairly confident that the paper's core internal claims are correct within the experimental setup described (seq2seq-to-SQL viability, integrated pipeline works in a small live demo, paraphrasing helps). Confidence is lower for broad operational and generalization claims due to small live sample size, optimistic simulations (oracle feedback), and missing quantitative operational metrics (crowd cost/latency, TF-IDF ablations).
